title: Projectile motion; Friction; Drag and terminal velocity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: D11-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; K04-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; D05-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; K04-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D05-1#N.11b, D11-1#N.3, D11-1#N.7, D11-1#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Fluid
items.clue: Any liquid or gas through which an object moves.

items.label: Range
items.clue: Horizontal distance a projectile covers between launch and landing.

items.label: Friction
items.clue: Acts parallel to two touching surfaces, opposing slipping between them.

items.label: Horizontal component
items.clue: Part of the launch velocity that never changes, as no force acts that way.

questions.stem: A box sits on the flat floor of a van. The van speeds up forwards along a straight, level road, and the box does not slide on the floor. Which statement about the friction force on the box is correct?

options.text: It acts backwards, because friction always opposes the box's motion.
There is no friction force, because the box is not sliding on the floor.
It acts forwards, and it is the force that makes the box speed up.
It acts forwards, but an equal backward force balances it.

questions.explanation: The box speeds up with the van, so it needs a forward resultant force. The only horizontal force on it is friction from the floor, so friction acts forwards.

questions.stem: A small steel ball is released from rest in air and falls until it reaches terminal velocity. How does its acceleration change during this time?

options.text: It is constant but less than g, because drag is constant.
It stays equal to g, since drag only lowers the ball's speed.
It increases, since the ball moves faster and faster as it falls.
It decreases from g towards zero as the drag increases.

questions.explanation: At release the ball is at rest, so there is no drag and its acceleration is g. As it speeds up the drag grows, so the acceleration decreases, reaching zero at terminal velocity.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown at an angle in air. Its path comes down more steeply than it went up. What is the main reason?

options.text: Gravity pulls harder on the ball as it falls than as it rises, so it drops more steeply.
Drag keeps reducing the horizontal velocity, so it is smaller on the way down.
Drag acts only after the top of the path, when the ball's speed starts to increase again.
The ball loses all of its horizontal velocity at the top, so it falls almost straight down.

questions.explanation: Drag opposes the velocity for the whole flight, so the horizontal velocity falls all the time. Coming down, the ball covers less ground for each metre it falls: a steeper path.

questions.stem: Two paper cones have the same size and shape. A second cone is pushed inside one of them, doubling its mass without changing its outside shape. Both are dropped from a high balcony. Which statement about their terminal velocities is correct?

options.text: Both reach the same terminal velocity, as all objects in free fall have the same acceleration.
The double cone reaches a higher terminal velocity, as drag must grow to equal a weight twice as large.
The double cone reaches a lower terminal velocity, as its greater weight gives it more drag at every speed.
The double cone reaches its terminal velocity sooner, as its greater weight gives it a greater acceleration from the start.
